home.brief.body: Live readings answer what's in the air right now. The evidence brief answers the harder question: why has Bali been left with so little visibility over its own air, and what will it take to fix it? A dossier of monitors, gaps, and the regulatory turning point of April 2026.

setup.deck: There are fifteen public air-quality sensors across Bali at the time of writing. The island has 4.4 million residents and 5,780 km². The argument for adding one more is straightforward: every additional monitor turns a guess into a number, and a number is the only thing a regulator, a school, or a journalist can act on.
setup.argA: The cheapest reliable PM2.5 sensor capable of contributing to a public network costs about as much as a long weekend in Seminyak. The data it produces — once it joins one of the international platforms — is auditable, timestamped, and impossible to politely walk back. It becomes part of the historical record this site already aggregates.
setup.argB: Bali's monitoring blind spots are not the fault of any one platform. They are the cumulative absence of small decisions to install. North Bali (Lovina, Singaraja), the eastern regencies (Karangasem, Amlapura), and the inland mountain belt (Bedugul, Kintamani) currently appear in our data as silence. A single sensor in any of those places would change that.
setup.argC: What follows is a short comparison of the four platforms most practical for Bali, then a generic install checklist that applies to all four.

disp.1.title: Two in three days, the daily guideline is exceeded.
disp.1.lede: A community sensor in Kerobokan logged four hundred and sixty-nine days of Bali's breath before it fell silent on 15 March — and on roughly two in three of them, the twenty-four-hour reading was above the line the World Health Organization now sets for a single day's exposure.

disp.4.lede: When the World Health Organization halved its safe-exposure ceiling for fine particulate matter in 2021, it did so because the underlying epidemiology had stopped finding a floor. The harm scales with the dose; the dose is what we breathe.

brief.headline: After the landfill ban, what happened to the air?
brief.deck: The island's only government air quality station in Denpasar has been dark since August 2025. Seven other monitors — all we can find — tell a consistent story: the particulate matter load across populated Bali routinely exceeds every international guideline.

disp.1.body.p1: The only long-running public record of Bali's air is a single community instrument on the back of a house in Kerobokan. It is a GAIA A12 laser-scatter sensor, corrected by the AQICN network, and since November 2024 it has posted a daily median to a page almost no one reads. Across its 469 days of operation, the mean reading reached 21.9 µg/m³ of PM2.5 — more than four times the World Health Organization's annual guideline of 5 µg/m³.
disp.1.body.p2: On roughly two of every three days of that record, the daily median was above the 15 µg/m³ ceiling the WHO set for a single day's exposure. On the fifteenth of March 2026, without announcement, the sensor fell silent.
disp.1.body.p3: The WHO's 2021 global air-quality guidelines lowered the twenty-four-hour PM2.5 threshold from the 25 µg/m³ it had set in 2005 to 15. The tightening reflected a body of epidemiological evidence that had, in the intervening decade, continued to tie moderate exposure to cardiovascular and respiratory harm. Indonesia's national ambient standard, codified in Peraturan Pemerintah 22 of 2021, remained at 55 µg/m³. Under domestic law, most of Bali's bad-air days are still formally normal.
disp.1.body.p4: There are two difficulties with the Kerobokan record. The first is the instrument itself. A laser-scatter sensor — however carefully corrected against a reference-grade monitor — is at the absolute end an indicator rather than a regulatory finding. Its numbers carry a slack of perhaps a few micrograms per cubic metre in either direction.
disp.1.body.p5: The second difficulty is the harder one. No one has built a reference-grade record against which the community figure could be checked. The island has one such government instrument — in Denpasar — and through 2025 it reported sporadically, and then not at all. (See Dispatch II.)
disp.1.body.p6: Indonesia's population-weighted annual PM2.5 in 2024, according to IQAir's World Air Quality Report, was 35.5 µg/m³, ranking the country fifteenth in the world. Bali's annual mean sits lower than Jakarta's. It is not the worst air in the country. But the 5 µg/m³ guideline was written at that level for a reason — and on an island that sells its climate as the product, two-thirds of days above 15 is a number that deserves to be recorded. The Kerobokan sensor was, at the time of writing, the only one keeping count.
disp.1.fig.l1: Days of continuous daily median PM2.5 reporting from the Kerobokan sensor, 21 Nov 2024 – 15 Mar 2026.
disp.1.fig.l2: Mean daily median across the 469-day record. The WHO annual guideline is 5 µg/m³; the 24-hour ceiling is 15.
disp.1.fig.l3: Share of days on which the daily median exceeded the WHO 15 µg/m³ 24-hour guideline. Dispatch analysis of the AQICN daily feed; raw CSV in Appendix.
disp.1.fig.l4: Mean daily reading as a multiple of the WHO 5 µg/m³ annual guideline. Indonesia's national standard remains 55.
disp.1.body.p7: What does two in three days mean, lived? It means that a child born in Kerobokan on the day the sensor began breathing the Bali average has, by her first birthday, received roughly twice the WHO-recommended annual dose. It means that on any given week of her life, four of its days will meet the short-term ceiling an international body considers a line of public-health consequence — and three of those four will exceed it.
disp.1.body.p8: Record is the quiet thing that is absent. When the Denpasar government sensor reports, it publishes an hourly AQI and a twenty-four-hour PM2.5 reading; when it does not, there is nothing on the national ISPU dashboard for the island. And on the one private long-record available, the daily guideline has been routinely exceeded for a year and a half.
disp.1.body.p9: A laser-scatter sensor, again, is not a regulatory instrument. The Kerobokan data is an indicator. Its 68 % figure is a Dispatch analysis of AQICN's public daily feed, and the raw CSV sits alongside this page in the Appendix so that anyone with a spreadsheet can reproduce it. The sensor is not reference-grade. That is the whole problem. For the island of Bali, in April of 2026, this is the best long-running public record that exists.
disp.1.body.p10: The instrument that should have been standing beside it — the government station in Denpasar, designed and maintained for exactly this purpose — has not posted to the ISPU portal in months. That is the subject of the next dispatch.
disp.2.body.p1: Bali's projected 2025 population, according to BPS Statistics Indonesia, is 4.46 million. The number of KLHK reference-grade PM2.5 monitors serving that population, indexed on the national ISPU portal, is one. That sensor, at Denpasar Lumintang on Jalan Mulawarman, reported sporadically through 2025 and, as of the first quarter of 2026, has not appeared on the portal in months.
disp.2.body.p2: Jakarta, for comparison, operates 10 reference-grade sensors and some 110 low-cost community monitors through its DKI programme, according to the 2024 Indonesia Air Quality report from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. Hong Kong runs 18 fixed stations for 7.5 million residents; London more than 100 continuous sites on its Local Air Quality Network. Bangkok's PCD runs 70 standard stations.
disp.2.body.p3: On a per-capita basis — government reference-grade sensors per million residents — Bali runs at roughly 0.2. Jakarta at 11. London at 11. Hong Kong at 2.4. Bangkok at about 4.5.
disp.2.body.p4: The CREA report, in its summary of provincial coverage outside of Jakarta, described "a significant coverage gap beyond the city limits into other satellite cities." Bali is one of those gaps. The Denpasar Lumintang station is not, let it be said, a failure of engineering. It is operated by the Environmental Laboratory Unit of the city's Environmental Health and Cleanliness Service under the national ISPUNet programme; when it runs, it publishes hourly AQI and 24-hour PM2.5 readings in the international format.
disp.2.body.p5: There is a temptation to treat community sensors (AQICN, Nafas, AirGradient, PurpleAir) as a substitute for government ones. The difficulty with the substitution is not that the private data is bad. It is that public record requires public accountability, and public accountability requires instruments whose calibration, maintenance, and placement are the obligation of an official body, not the citizens it represents.
disp.2.body.p6: Reference-grade government instruments only. Community and private sensors (AQICN, Nafas, AirGradient, PurpleAir) are not included. Sources in the footer of this dispatch.
disp.2.body.p7: When the Denpasar Lumintang instrument is running, it speaks. When it is not, the island's official record is silent — not because there are no pollutants to measure, but because there is no government instrument to measure them with. The community data, as Dispatch I set out, is the best long-running public record in the absence of the government one. It is an imperfect stand-in.
disp.2.body.p8: The proposal — it is not a new one — is modest. A handful of reference-grade monitors at Denpasar, Ubud, Canggu, Seminyak, Nusa Dua and either Singaraja or Amed. A public dashboard on the ISPU portal, updated hourly, with a clean CSV backlog for researchers. An annual uptime report, on the London LAQN model. A budget line in the provincial Dinas Lingkungan Hidup that protects these instruments from the routine budgetary losses that have taken down the Denpasar unit.
disp.2.body.p9: The next dispatch, on what has happened since the first of April, is an argument for why that choice matters now and not later.
disp.3.body.p1: On the first of April 2026 the new Denpasar waste rule took effect: no sorted waste, no collection. In Badung regency, the penalty for non-compliance reaches Rp 25 million and three months' imprisonment. The rule's stated purpose — and it is a good one — is to force the separation stream that will allow the long-troubled Suwung landfill, handling around 1,000 tonnes of mixed waste a day, to stop accepting organics and, eventually, on 1 August, to close.
disp.3.body.p2: Two weeks in, the consequence was a different one. Denpasar's Public Works and Spatial Planning Office (PUPR) reported in mid-April that up to seven tons of waste a day were being pulled from the city's rivers by municipal crews — a figure attributed by Hey Bali News to Ketut Ngurah Artha Jaya, the office's head of water resources. Sungai Watch, the river-cleanup organisation that separately processes about three tons of plastic a day at its headquarters, flagged a visible post-1-April surge.
disp.3.body.p3: And down the gangs of Sanur, Kuta and Canggu, the smoke — the domestic kind, the kind made by burning what ought to have been collected — became a matter of everyday observation. Surfers at Uluwatu posted air-quality-alarmed videos. Community sensors logged US-AQI spikes as high as 150, the threshold at which "unhealthy for everyone" begins.
disp.3.body.p4: Open household burning is a recognised and locally dominant PM2.5 source in Indonesian communities with incomplete collection coverage, according to the Climate & Clean Air Coalition's CLOCC programme for Indonesia. The science is old; the policy mechanism is obvious. Where collection fails, the residue is burned. What is new, and specific to Bali, is that the burning is now rising in the absence of any reference-grade monitoring to characterise it.
disp.3.body.p5: Governor Wayan Koster, asked about the burning, distinguished between religious ritual and domestic refuse: "If it's wood or bamboo from religious offerings, that's not a problem." Mayor I Gusti Ngurah Jaya Negara of Denpasar declared that there would be "no more community-level burning", and that existing facilities would absorb the unsorted stream. The infrastructure to do so, at present, is not visibly in place. Nor are the sensors to measure the cost of its absence.
disp.3.body.p6: Ayu Pawitri of Get Plastic Indonesia, quoted in Hey Bali News, named the structural point: the ban is the right policy; the bottleneck is the missing composting infrastructure, not the rule itself. A sorting rule, without a place for the sorted output to go, produces exactly the post-1-April pattern the island is now seeing.
disp.3.fig.l1: Denpasar's new rule: no sorted waste, no collection. Badung penalty up to Rp 25 million & 3 months' imprisonment.
disp.3.fig.l2: River waste pulled from Denpasar's rivers by municipal crews in mid-April 2026, per the city's PUPR. Distinct from Sungai Watch's separate ~3 t/day HQ processing figure.
disp.3.fig.l3: Pre-ban Suwung landfill throughput. Organics ≈ two-thirds of Bali's waste stream. Landfill permanent closure scheduled for 1 August 2026.
disp.3.fig.l4: Community-sensor peak US-AQI readings from Kuta, Canggu and Uluwatu in the first two weeks of April — the threshold at which "unhealthy for everyone" begins.
disp.3.body.p7: The correlation between rising burning and the community-sensor PM2.5 spikes is, at the moment, suggestive rather than proven. Community sensors are laser-scatter devices; their absolute numbers carry slack; 150-US-AQI spikes could have other contributing sources — vehicular, construction, agricultural, even Nyepi-adjacent offerings. This is precisely the kind of question a reference-grade government network is designed to settle, by cross-comparing hourly readings at multiple fixed sites. The Denpasar Lumintang station, which could have settled it, has not reported in months.
disp.3.body.p8: The cost of that absence is the cost of a policy argument that has to be made without numbers. The 1 April rule is defensible on its own terms — organics at Suwung are a genuine problem, the landfill's closure is long overdue — but its early consequences, in the absence of an air-quality record, are a matter of anecdote and photograph rather than fact.
disp.3.body.p9: The Kerobokan sensor was one citizen's private record, made public at private cost. The Denpasar sensor has been a public record, reported to the public only intermittently. The island of Bali, on the morning these dispatches were filed, has no reference-grade air quality measurement being published to any national portal. That is the shape of the gap. The fix is modest. The cost is small. The moment — with burning rising and the landfill rule still young — is now.
disp.4.body.p1: For every additional ten micrograms a cubic metre of long-term PM2.5, pooled meta-analyses commissioned for the WHO 2021 guideline review report a 9.5% increase in all-cause mortality, a 12.7% rise in circulatory mortality, a 14.3% rise in ischaemic heart disease mortality, a 14.6% rise in cerebrovascular mortality, a 13.8% rise in mortality from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a 9.3% rise in lung-cancer mortality. The all-cause estimate alone implies an attributable fraction of about 8.7% per ten-microgram increment, if the association is causal.
disp.4.body.p2: These are not edge-case findings. The Global Burden of Disease project attributes more than four million deaths in 2019 to long-term ambient PM2.5. A separate global modelling study estimates that the open burning of domestic waste alone — the activity overhanging Bali in April of 2026 — produces roughly 270,000 premature deaths a year, although that source-specific figure assumes the toxicity per microgram is the same as that of average urban PM2.5. The toxicology suggests it is probably worse.
disp.4.body.p3: Plastic and household-waste smoke is chemically distinct from typical urban PM. It is dominated by carbon — more than seventy per cent in one source-profile study — and enriched in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, polychlorinated and polybrominated dioxins and furans, and transition metals including lead, cadmium, chromium, nickel, copper, zinc, and antimony. Co-emitted gases include benzene, styrene, formaldehyde, vinyl chloride, and 1,3-butadiene. The mixture has high oxidative potential and contains environmentally persistent free radicals; in cell-free assays it generates hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals, and reactive chlorine species.
disp.4.body.p4: The mechanism is not mysterious. Inhaled PM2.5 deposits in the deep lung. From there it triggers oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, with vascular endothelial dysfunction and autonomic-nervous-system imbalance following on. The downstream pathology spans cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, cancer, and — increasingly — the nervous system. A 2022 meta-analysis reported a 40 per cent increase in dementia risk per ten micrograms of long-term PM2.5; a more conservative 2025 burden-of-proof analysis reports at least a fourteen per cent average increase across the range of exposures observed in the published cohorts. For autism-spectrum disorder, the prenatal-exposure literature suggests a thirty-one per cent increase per ten micrograms during pregnancy and sixty-four per cent during early childhood.
disp.4.body.p5: Pregnancy outcomes show a coherent dose response. A 2021 global meta-regression estimated that each ten-microgram rise in ambient PM2.5 during pregnancy reduces birth weight by twenty-two grams, raises low-birth-weight risk by eleven per cent, and raises preterm-birth risk by twelve per cent. These outcomes matter especially for the Bali context, because waste burning happens close to homes, repeats episodically, and falls hardest on neighbourhoods without formal collection.
disp.4.body.p6: The Kerobokan sensor recorded a 469-day mean of 21.9 µg/m³ — sixteen-point-nine micrograms above the WHO five-microgram annual guideline. Applied naively to the all-cause coefficient, that delta corresponds to roughly a fifteen per cent excess long-term mortality risk, if the relationship holds at this concentration band. The honest caveat is that the published coefficients are for total ambient PM2.5; the source-specific coefficient for plastic-burning PM has not been estimated. Multiple lines of toxicology suggest the true number is probably higher.
disp.4.fig.l1: All-cause mortality attributable fraction per ten-microgram-per-cubic-metre increment in long-term PM2.5. Pooled estimate from the WHO 2021-aligned meta-analysis.
disp.4.fig.l2: Excess ischaemic-heart-disease mortality per ten-microgram-per-cubic-metre rise. One of the largest single-cause coefficients in the pooled record.
disp.4.fig.l3: Estimated annual premature deaths globally attributable to PM2.5 from open burning of domestic waste, per CCAC-aligned modelling. Source-equal-toxicity assumption is conservative.
disp.4.fig.l4: Approximate excess all-cause mortality risk implied by Kerobokan's 21.9 µg/m³ mean against the WHO 5 µg/m³ annual guideline, applying the pooled coefficient. Plastic-burning PM is plausibly more harmful per microgram than this estimate.
disp.4.body.p7: The vulnerable populations are the predictable ones: children, pregnant people and their fetuses, older adults, anyone with pre-existing cardiopulmonary disease, informal waste workers, and the residents of neighbourhoods without reliable collection. Lower socioeconomic status amplifies the risk through cumulative exposure and reduced access to filtration, medical care, and the option to leave. Across the cohort literature, no clear threshold has been established below which chronic cardiovascular harm disappears.
disp.4.body.p8: The 2021 guideline of five micrograms a cubic metre — and the twenty-four-hour ceiling of fifteen — were not picked at random. They were the level at which the meta-analyses stopped showing improvement with further reductions in exposure. Indonesia's national ambient standard, codified in Peraturan Pemerintah 22 of 2021, remains at fifty-five micrograms. Under domestic law, most of Bali's bad-air days are still formally normal.
disp.4.sub.2: What the published evidence does not tell you.
disp.4.body.p9: The strongest limitation in the literature is that almost every long-term effect estimate is for total ambient PM2.5, not for the fraction specifically derived from plastic and household waste burning. Source-resolved cohort studies near open burns do not yet exist at scale; toxicology suggests the per-microgram harm is worse than average; the actual coefficient is unspecified.
disp.4.body.p10: For the purposes of this dispatch, the prudent reading is that chronic exposure to PM2.5 from burning plastics and household waste is unlikely to be safer than typical urban PM2.5, and may be substantially more harmful per unit mass. The exact excess risk in Bali — over a Bali-specific population, over multi-year follow-up, with adjustment for tobacco and cooking exposure — has not been measured. The first step toward measuring it is the same as the first step toward fixing it: a denser network of monitors than this island currently has.
disp.5.body.p1: When you're picking a mask for daily scooter rides or smoky days, the standard matters most. Look for masks rated N95, KN95, KF94, FFP2, FFP3, or P2 — these have been independently tested to filter fine particulate matter. Cloth and fabric masks aren't designed to filter smoke or exhaust. Beyond the rating, a good mask needs a snug fit, comfortable breathing for Bali's heat, and an affordable filter-replacement habit you'll actually keep up with.
disp.5.sub.1: A short recommendation, by use case.
disp.5.body.p4: A note on the science baseline: an N95 respirator is tested to filter at least 95 % of certain non-oil airborne particles. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health emphasises that fit is essential — even a NIOSH-certified mask filters poorly if it does not seal closely to the face.
disp.5.sub.3: Indoors, the mask is your air conditioner.
disp.5.body.p7: Three small habits make a measurable difference. Keep AC filters clean — a clogged split-unit filter recirculates dust rather than clearing it; pull the front cover, rinse the foam mesh in warm water, dry, and replace, ideally once a fortnight in burning season. Run a HEPA air purifier in the bedroom and main living space; even a single mid-range unit (Xiaomi, IKEA, Coway, Levoit, BlueAir — anything rated for PM2.5 with a true-HEPA filter) cuts indoor PM2.5 dramatically when the windows are closed. Close the windows when the air outside is bad; this site exists in part to make that decision easier.
brief.body.p1: In April 2026, Bali's regulations on organic waste disposal were tightened. The Suwung landfill, long the island's primary waste endpoint, stopped accepting organic material. In the weeks that followed, residents across Ubud, Kerobokan, Canggu and Jimbaran reported a marked increase in the smell and visible presence of burning waste — particularly in the early morning and after dark.
brief.body.p2: This document sets out what the available air quality monitoring records can and cannot tell us about that change. It is written for journalists, researchers, and residents who want to verify the numbers themselves.
brief.body.p3: Public historical data exists for only a handful of Bali air quality monitors. The AQICN network preserves records for the Denpasar government KLHK station (548 days, offline since August 2025) and the Kerobokan community sensor (469 days, now reporting again through IQAir). OpenAQ preserves CSVs for three additional private AirGradient sensors in Ubud, Balangan and Kopernik — all now offline as well.
brief.body.p4: Two PurpleAir units in Klungkung and Jimbaran are still reporting. Between them, they cover roughly two years of continuous data.
brief.body.p5: Bali has no distributed public air quality monitoring network. There is no multi-year record for Sanur, North Bali, or East Bali. There is no open data feed from the provincial government. There is no requirement for industrial, hospitality, or municipal operators to publish ambient readings.
brief.body.p6: What exists is a patchwork of privately-owned devices, voluntarily shared through platforms that happen to have open APIs. This document's purpose is to make that patchwork legible.
brief.body.q1: "Without distributed monitoring, it is impossible to determine whether the patterns seen in Kerobokan and Denpasar are representative of the island as a whole."

brief.x.ch2pB1: The Kerobokan community sensor, part of the AQICN / GAIA network, recorded 469 days from November 2024 to March 2026. Its public AQICN feed went quiet on the 15th of March — two weeks before organic waste was banned from the Suwung landfill — though the same device has since resumed reporting through IQAir.
brief.x.ch2pB2: The sensor is privately owned. The record it left behind during that window — daily medians averaging 21.9 µg/m³, with 68% of days exceeding the WHO 24-hour guideline — remains one of the most detailed openly downloadable windows we have into the air above south Bali.

disp.7.title: Ninety days of data on the island's garbage fires.
disp.7.lede: Bali Air Dispatch · 20 July 2026 · The first data review since Dispatch VI
disp.7.body.p1: Our last dispatch went out in April, as the dry season began and this register was still small. Since 17 April the network has grown to twenty-plus live sensors across seven networks and has logged roughly two thousand sensor-days of PM2.5 — the island's air, measured every fifteen minutes, in the first dry season under Bali's new waste rules.
disp.7.body.p2: We built this network to answer one question: what is the routine open burning of garbage doing to the air Balinese families breathe? Ninety days in, the data has begun to answer — in the numbers, and, more tellingly, in the clock.
disp.7.sub.2: § IIThe season turned, and it is worse than last year
disp.7.body.p3: The island-wide picture, month by month (mean of every archived sensor-day; the WHO 24-hour guideline is 15 µg/m³):
disp.7.body.p4: A caveat we owe the reader: the sensor mix changed as the network grew, so monthly means partly reflect where coverage was added. The cleaner test holds one sensor constant. At Bali Umalas (Villa Fusion) — a residential neighbourhood sensor archived continuously since November 2024, nowhere near a rice field — the same 1 June–20 July window reads: 2025, mean 26.2 µg/m³, 92% of days over the guideline. 2026, mean 31.4 µg/m³, 100% of days over. At the one sensor able to compare, this season runs about a fifth dirtier than last year's, and not one day since June began has met the WHO guideline.
disp.7.sub.3: § IIIThe clock evidence: smoke on a household schedule
disp.7.body.p5: If the island's smoke came mainly from a seasonal agricultural event, the record would show broad daytime plumes where the harvest is. It shows something else: a twice-daily rhythm, everywhere, on the clock of domestic life.
disp.7.body.p6: Averaging every 15-minute reading since 17 April by hour of day (WITA), at two kinds of sensor held constant all season:
disp.7.body.p7: Two peaks, the same two peaks, at every sensor: a morning maximum at 08:00–09:00 — when household rubbish fires are lit and the night's accumulated smoke still sits trapped under the overnight inversion layer — and an evening climb from 19:00 as the day's second round of burning starts and the air stills again. The cleanest air of the day is mid-afternoon, when burning pauses and the sea breeze and daytime heat stir the boundary layer.
disp.7.body.p8: This is not the signature of a harvest. It is the signature of a chore — the daily, island-wide routine of burning mixed household waste in yards, roadsides, ditches and field edges, morning and evening, seven days a week. The rural western sensors show the same schedule at higher amplitude: more fires, bigger piles, stiller air — and, as anyone who has walked a field edge knows, those piles are rarely crop residue alone. Plastic, packaging and household rubbish are burned alongside whatever else is at hand.
disp.7.body.p9: The practical reading is blunt. The worst hour of the day is nine in the morning — the school run, the market run, the commute. The "fresh morning air" instinct has it exactly backwards in burn season. The clean window is roughly 14:00–17:00.
disp.7.x.pullQ: "The smoke keeps house hours — morning and evening, everywhere at once — the schedule of garbage fires, or larger burn sites, not of any harvest."
disp.7.body.p10: The heaviest validated days since 17 April belong to ten different stations in every corner of the island — city, suburb, and countryside:
disp.7.body.p11: Days at 90–165 µg/m³ are six to eleven times the WHO daily guideline. (A community sensor in Tabanan's rice country recorded days higher still, up to 162; its calibration is unverified, so we leave it out of the tables — but its direction agrees with the validated Tabanan and Umadawa stations beside it.)
disp.7.body.p12: And the residential burden is constant, not episodic. Since mid-April: Umalas exceeded the WHO daily guideline on 95% of days (mean 27.6), Sidakarya in south Denpasar on 82% (mean 23.0), Kopernik in Mas, Ubud on 74% (mean 24.2) — with instantaneous readings in Ubud as high as 133 µg/m³. These are neighbourhoods of homes, schools and warungs. Nobody is harvesting rice in Umalas.
disp.7.sub.5: § VWhat we can and cannot claim
disp.7.body.p13: A PM2.5 sensor weighs smoke; it cannot chemically tell burning plastic from burning straw. The remarkable consistency of the morning and evening peaks across multiple regions suggests widespread combustion sources operating on similar daily schedules.
disp.7.body.p14: Determining the relative contribution of household burning, village waste-processing facilities, agricultural burning and other sources is the next stage of the analysis.
disp.7.sub.6: § VIThe network itself: what died watching
disp.7.body.p15: Ninety days of measurement cost us machines. The Nafas network in Bali went dark station by station — Pemogan on 13 June, Sanur and Ubud on 16 June, and Tonja, the station that recorded the island's worst day, on 1 July. Nafas stations elsewhere in Indonesia update normally; the withdrawal is Bali-specific, and it removed what was once the island's best consumer network mid-season. Their final readings are preserved here, and co-located failover feeds now cover two of the sites. The Jimbaran Smart Citizen cluster also left the outdoor record in June–July.
disp.7.body.p16: Against the losses: hourly records from ten IQAir stations, a second government-adjacent station, and a direct line to the AirGradient community network.
disp.7.sub.7: § VIIWhat the data is telling us
disp.7.step.1.lab: The air is worse than last year
disp.7.step.1.body: — about a fifth dirtier at the one sensor that can compare seasons, with residential neighbourhoods over the WHO daily guideline nine days in ten.
disp.7.step.2.lab: The dominant pattern is domestic or industrial, not agricultural.
disp.7.step.2.body: The smoke keeps house hours — morning and evening, everywhere at once — the schedule of garbage fires, not of any harvest.
disp.7.step.3.lab: Exposure is worst when people are most exposed.
disp.7.step.3.body: The 08:00–09:00 peak coincides with school runs and markets. Shifting outdoor exercise, ventilation and children's travel toward the 14:00–17:00 window is free and cuts the daily dose materially.
disp.7.step.4.lab: The record is fragile exactly where it matters.
disp.7.step.4.body: The stations that recorded the worst air kept dying, and a commercial network withdrew mid-season. The next step is more independent sensors in more hands — especially beside the burn sites themselves — with every record preserved when the hardware fails.
disp.7.close.p1: Every number in this dispatch is drawn from the archive and can be re-derived from it and every silenced sensor's record stays on the history page.
articles.x.row7Title: Ninety days of data on the island's garbage fires.
articles.x.row7Deck: The register's first full review — twenty-plus live sensors, roughly two thousand sensor-days of PM2.5, the first dry season under the new waste rules. The season runs about a fifth dirtier than last year at the one sensor able to compare, and the smoke keeps house hours: peaking at nine in the morning, everywhere at once. The signature of a chore, not a harvest.
articles.x.sub: An index of the dispatches — seven readings from the unmonitored island.
articles.x.leadDeck: A community sensor logged four hundred and sixty-nine days of Bali's breath before it fell silent. A single government monitor reports intermittently for 4.4 million residents. Since the first of April, seven tons of waste a day have been pulled from Denpasar's rivers. The smoke in the alleys rises without an instrument to record it. The science underneath, the practical mask guide, what would actually help, in the order it should be deployed — and now, ninety days into the burn season, the first full data review: what the network actually recorded.
home.h.d7: Ninety days of data — on the island's garbage fires.
home.d7.body: Two thousand sensor-days across seven networks, read end to end. The record keeps house hours — a spike at nine in the morning, a second climb after dark, everywhere on the island at once. That is the schedule of household waste fires, not of any harvest. And this dry season is running dirtier than last year's.
home.d7.stat: of days since June exceeded the WHO 24-hour guideline at the one sensor with a two-year record — up from 92% in the same window last year.
disp.7.sub.8: § VIIIWhat would help most now
disp.7.body.p17: Answering the question this dispatch leaves open takes more sensors, in more places. Every additional monitor turns an assumption into a measurement, and the blank areas on our map — the north, the east, the mountain villages, and the burn sites themselves — are simply places where nobody has installed one yet. A basic outdoor unit costs about what a weekend away does, publishes automatically to the open networks this site reads, and joins the public record here within minutes of coming online. If you can host one, the setup guide is here.
appx.M.title: How the readings are processed
appx.M.lede: Most sensors on this map are shown exactly as their network reports them. Two networks are humidity-corrected before display. This is what we change, and why.
appx.x.mP1: Why any correction at all. Low-cost PM2.5 sensors size particles by shining a laser through the air, so in humid conditions water-swollen particles scatter more light and the sensor reads more mass than is really there. Bali runs 45–70% relative humidity, where this over-read is large. The two community networks built on Plantower modules — AirGradient and PurpleAir — publish this uncorrected figure on the open feeds we read, so we apply the standard humidity correction ourselves before showing it. Every other network on the map (Nafas, AQICN, IQAir, Smart Citizen, OpenAQ) is displayed as supplied.
appx.x.mP2: The formula. We use the US EPA 2021 correction for Plantower/PurpleAir sensors — the same algorithm AirGradient applies to produce the “compensated” value on its own dashboard, which their public feed does not expose. It adjusts the raw reading using the sensor's own relative-humidity measurement, in five concentration bands. Our version is the EPA formula only; AirGradient's dashboard adds a small per-device factory calibration that is not published, so our corrected values track theirs closely but are not identical.
appx.x.mP3: What it does to the numbers. The correction is mostly downward and can be substantial — in humid, smoky conditions a raw 28 µg/m³ becomes roughly 15. It is not downward everywhere: the formula carries a fixed offset, so in very clean, drier air a near-zero raw reading is lifted to about 2 µg/m³. That floor is a known property of the published regression at the bottom of its range, not a fault in the sensor; readings that low are already well within the “Good” band and the distinction has no health meaning. We publish the corrected value as-is rather than hiding this behaviour.
appx.x.mP4: Provenance and reversibility. The raw figure is stored alongside every corrected reading, so the correction is fully auditable and reversible and nothing a sensor actually reported is lost. Correction began on 21 July 2026; earlier readings from these networks remain as they were recorded. PurpleAir history before that date stays uncorrected because we did not previously store the humidity needed to correct it, so a PurpleAir sensor's own record shows a small one-time step at the changeover. A · corrected tag marks any reading this has been applied to.

api.mast.sub: The whole archive, open to anyone who asks for it. No key, no account, no conditions beyond attribution.
api.mast.title: The API
api.x.aP1: This is a read-only interface onto an aggregated archive of Bali air-quality measurements — PM2.5 and its companion values — collected from public sensor networks since 2025. It exists so that nobody has to scrape this site. The archive runs to roughly 140,000 rows in total, which means a patient client can hold all of it locally in a few minutes.
api.x.aP2: Eight networks are aggregated here: Nafas, IQAir, PurpleAir, AQICN, OpenAQ, AirGradient, Smart Citizen and Airly. Each row names the network it came from, so a result can always be traced back to its origin and checked against that network's own feed.
api.x.aP3: Every route is GET only and returns permissive CORS headers, so browser code may call it directly from any origin. Responses are edge-cached for between five and sixty minutes depending on how fast the underlying data moves; one served out of that cache carries X-Cache: HIT. There is no key, no account and no rate limit beyond fair use — the row caps below are the only enforcement.
api.x.aP4: What this is not. Low-cost sensors are not reference-grade instruments. Values are published as they were recorded, without warranty of accuracy or fitness for any purpose. Chapter E is the part to read before you average anything.
api.x.buildP1: If you make something with this — a study, a chart, a bot, a school project, a better map than ours — we would genuinely like to know. Not for credit; because knowing what the data is used for tells us what to collect next, and because someone else in the community is probably trying to do the same thing.
api.x.buildP2: The WhatsApp community is the fastest way to reach the people using this data, and the address in the footer works for anything longer. Bug reports on the interface itself are especially welcome: if a field is wrong, a cursor misbehaves or this page contradicts what the API actually does, that is a defect and we will fix it.
api.x.buildP3: If you would rather add to the record than read it, the gaps on the map are simply places nobody has installed a sensor yet — the setup guide is here.
api.x.cP1: Knowing which store answered. Every /measurements response carries source_table, naming the store the rows came out of. Naming a station gives you a single store — station_daily, station_snapshots, station_snapshots (hourly buckets), nafas_daily, nafas_hourly, iq_scrape_daily or iq_scrape_hourly. A bulk scan unions several, and says so in the same field: station_daily + nafas_daily + iq_scrape_daily for bulk daily, and station_snapshots (hourly buckets) + nafas_hourly + iq_scrape_hourly for bulk hourly. Bulk raw is the single-store case, station_snapshots. You never have to know this to use the interface — the row shape is identical either way — but it means any result you publish can be traced back to specific tables.
api.x.cP2: Where min, max and samples are null. Networks that publish pre-aggregated hourly or daily figures give us one number per bucket, not a distribution, so pm25_min, pm25_max and samples come back null for those rows: pm25_min and pm25_max are null on every Nafas and scraped-IQAir row, and samples is null on every Nafas row and on scraped-IQAir hourly rows, though scraped-IQAir daily rows do carry a count where the scrape recorded one. Where the bucket was computed here from raw snapshots, all three are populated. A null is an honest absence, never a zero; and a populated samples of 1 is not the same thing as a null — see Chapter E.
api.x.call1: Index. Version, routes, parameters, interval definitions, caveats and licence.
api.x.call2: The catalogue. Every station, with coordinates, network, date coverage and provenance flags.
api.x.call3: A snapshot. The most recent reading held for each station, all networks at once.
api.x.call4: The time series. Raw, hourly or daily; one station or all of them; JSON or CSV; paged.
api.x.caveat1Label: 1 · Some of these sensors are indoors
api.x.caveat1P1: A monitor sitting in a clinic waiting room or a purified bedroom measures that room, not the island's air, and it will read far cleaner than the street outside. Those stations carry suspected_indoor: true on the station record and on every single measurement row, so a filter never needs a join.
api.x.caveat1P2: This site excludes them from every island-wide statistic it publishes. If you are averaging across stations, you should too. They are published rather than deleted because a suspected classification should be yours to disagree with — but an ambient analysis that silently includes them will understate Bali's air quality problem, and it will do so invisibly.
api.x.caveat4: Instants are UTC. Daily dates are WITA. This is the one place the interface is deliberately not uniform, and it will bite an analysis that assumes otherwise. Every instant — observed_at, first_seen, last_seen, generated_at, and the normalised from and to in the query block — is ISO-8601 UTC with a trailing Z. But a daily date is a WITA calendar day, WITA being UTC+8 all year with no daylight saving. Daily buckets are aggregated on the local day because that is the meaningful one for a Bali reader: household waste burning has a sharp morning peak and a second climb after dark, and a UTC day would cut that evening in half. Every /measurements response states which basis applies in date_basis, so you never have to guess. Convert instants to WITA before analysing time of day, and do not silently re-bucket the daily series onto UTC.
api.x.caveat5: Two networks are corrected, the rest are not, and only from a date. Low-cost optical sensors size particles with a laser, so in humid air water-swollen particles scatter more light and the sensor over-reads. AirGradient and PurpleAir publish that uncorrected figure on the open feeds we read, so we apply the standard US-EPA 2021 humidity correction before publication; every other network — Nafas, IQAir, AQICN, OpenAQ, Smart Citizen, Airly — is passed through exactly as supplied. The correction began on a specific date, which /stations reports per network as pm25_correction_applied_since, and it was not applied retroactively. The great majority of archived PurpleAir and AirGradient rows therefore predate it and carry pm25_corrected: false with a null pm25_raw — so a series that crosses that date is not corrected uniformly along its length. Nothing is lost either way: pm25_raw carries the original figure on every corrected reading, so you can reverse or re-derive the correction yourself. The formula and its behaviour at the bottom of its range are set out in the methodology chapter of the appendix.
api.x.ep1desc: The index. Returns the version, the route list with their parameters, the interval definitions, the semantic notes reproduced in Chapter E, and the licence. It takes no parameters and does not touch the archive, so it answers even if the database is briefly unreachable.
api.x.ep2desc: Every station in the archive. This is the catalogue you join everything else against: it is where station_id values come from, and where you learn which stations are flagged indoor, from which date their network's readings are humidity-corrected, and how many days of record each one holds. Placeholder catalogue rows the site never published are excluded here and from every bulk scan. Physical duplicates are not. Every Bali OpenAQ station is an AirGradient unit relayed through OpenAQ, so it also appears under its own ag- id at the same coordinates — two rows, one device. The archive keeps both on purpose: they are genuinely different records of that hardware, the ag- one instantaneous and humidity-corrected, the oq- one republished hourly and uncorrected. De-duplicate on coordinates before any island-wide aggregate, or you will count those devices twice.
api.x.ep3desc: The most recent reading held for every station — one row per station, all networks in a single call. This is what the live map on the front page is built from. Stations that have never reported a usable value are absent rather than present-and-empty. Every row carries age_hours and stale, because "latest" is not the same thing as "now".
api.x.ep4desc: The time series, and the route you will spend your time in. Name a station or omit it to scan every station at once; choose raw, hourly or daily; bound it by date; take it as JSON or CSV; page through it with a cursor.
api.x.ep4note1: Paging. A next_cursor appears only when the page filled to the limit — when it comes back null, you have reached the end. Naming a station gives a one-part cursor; omitting it gives a two-part cursor, because a bulk scan sorts by station and then by time. Treat the token as opaque and hand it back exactly as received.
api.x.ep4note2: Bulk scans. Omitting station scans every station in the archive, across all three storage families — the universal store, the Nafas tables and the scraped IQAir tables are unioned, so a bulk daily or hourly pull returns each station's real series rather than a shallow rollup. Placeholder catalogue rows are excluded. Physical duplicates are not: the ag- and oq- copies of one relayed device both appear, so de-duplicate on coordinates before aggregating or that device counts twice. A station you name explicitly is always served in full, whether or not it is one the site publishes.
api.x.errBadCursor: The cursor has the wrong number of components, an empty component, or an invalid station component. A single-station scan expects a one-part cursor and a bulk scan a two-part one, so a token cannot be moved between the two. Pass back next_cursor unmodified.
api.x.errBadFrom: from could not be read as a date, an ISO-8601 instant, or unix seconds.
api.x.errBadInterval: interval was not one of raw, hourly, daily.
api.x.errBadStation: station is not a well-formed station_id. Take the value from /stations rather than constructing it.
api.x.errBadTo: to could not be read as a date, an ISO-8601 instant, or unix seconds.
api.x.errInternal: Something failed on our side. No internal detail is echoed back — if it persists, tell us.
api.x.errMethod: Anything other than GET, HEAD or a CORS preflight. The interface is read-only.
api.x.errNoRaw: You asked for interval=raw on a scraped IQAir station. IQAir publishes hourly, so no sub-hourly series exists. Use hourly or daily.
api.x.errNotFound: Unknown route. The response lists the routes that do exist.
api.x.errP: Errors come back as JSON with a stable machine-readable error code and a human sentence in message. Branch on the code, show the message. Some errors carry extra keys — a bad interval for a scraped IQAir station also returns available_intervals, and an unknown route returns the list of routes that do exist.
api.x.errUnavailable: The archive is temporarily unreachable. Retry shortly; the index route keeps answering meanwhile.
api.x.fAqi: Air Quality Index as the originating network reported it. Networks differ in which scale they use, so do not compare AQI across sources — compare PM2.5.
api.x.fAqiMax: Highest AQI seen in the bucket, on the originating network's scale.
api.x.fCorrected2: True where this reading was humidity-corrected — which is exactly the rows carrying a pm25_raw. A per-row fact, not a network-wide one: most archived PurpleAir and AirGradient rows predate the correction and are false. Present on /latest and on interval=raw rows; aggregate rows do not carry it, because a bucket can straddle the changeover.
api.x.fCount: Number of rows in this response — this page, not the whole result set.
api.x.fDate: The day the bucket covers, as a WITA (UTC+8) calendar day — the local day, not the UTC one. Daily rows only. The response repeats this in date_basis.
api.x.fDays: Count of days present in the daily series. Zero means no daily rollup exists yet, not that the station is silent.
api.x.fError: Machine-readable failure code. Present only on errors, alongside message.
api.x.fFirstDate: Earliest day in the station's daily series. Can predate first_seen where history was backfilled.
api.x.fFirstSeen: When this archive first collected from the station. JSON only.
api.x.fGeneratedAt: When this snapshot was assembled. /latest only.
api.x.fHum: Relative humidity at the sensor. This is the input to the correction described in Chapter E.
api.x.fIndoor: True where the sensor appears to be measuring a room rather than ambient air. Read Chapter E before averaging anything.
api.x.fIndoor2: True where the sensor appears to be measuring a room rather than ambient air. Carried on every row so a filter never needs a join.
api.x.fIndoor3: True where the sensor appears to be measuring a room rather than ambient air.
api.x.fIntervalSource: Which storage family serves this station: universal, nafas or iqair_scrape. The last of these has no raw interval.
api.x.fLastDate: Most recent day in the station's daily series.
api.x.fLastSeen: When this archive last collected from the station. JSON only.
api.x.fLat: Decimal degrees, WGS 84. Negative in Bali.
api.x.fLicence: The four licence statements, repeated on every response so a saved file always carries its own terms.
api.x.fName: Station name as the originating network publishes it.
api.x.fNextCursor: Opaque continuation token, or null when this is the last page. /measurements JSON only — the CSV form puts it in X-Next-Cursor.
api.x.fObservedAt: When this archive recorded the reading. This is the field to sort and join on.
api.x.fObservedAtH: Start of the hour the bucket covers, in UTC. Hourly rows only.
api.x.fPm1: Particulate matter, 1 micrometre and below. Null on networks that do not publish it.
api.x.fPm10: Particulate matter, 10 micrometres and below. Null on networks that do not publish it.
api.x.fPm25: Fine particulate matter, 2.5 micrometres and below. The published value — humidity-corrected for AirGradient and PurpleAir, as-supplied for everyone else.
api.x.fPm25Max: Highest PM2.5 seen in the bucket. This is where short pollution events show up that a mean hides.
api.x.fPm25Min: Lowest PM2.5 seen in the bucket. Null where the store holds no distribution.
api.x.fPm25Raw: The uncorrected sensor figure, stored alongside every corrected reading so the correction is auditable and reversible. null where no correction was applied — which includes every row archived before the correction began, on corrected networks too.
api.x.fQuery: Your request as the interface understood it, with dates normalised. Check this first when a result surprises you. /measurements only.
api.x.fSamples: How many observations went into the mean. A low count is a thin average — weight it accordingly. 1 is common on older backfilled daily rows, where the mean, the minimum and the maximum are all the same single reading. null where the store holds no count at all, which is not the same as a count of zero.
api.x.fSource: The network the reading came from — Nafas, IQAir, PurpleAir, AQICN, OpenAQ, AirGradient, Smart Citizen or Airly.
api.x.fSourceTable: Which underlying store answered, or which stores were unioned on a bulk scan. /measurements only.
api.x.fStationId: Stable identifier, prefixed by network. Use it verbatim; do not construct it. Some contain spaces.
api.x.fType: Free-text device or ownership description from the network — government station, community sensor, and so on. Not a controlled vocabulary.
api.x.fUpstream: The timestamp the originating network attached to the same reading, where it gave one. Usually a minute or two before observed_at. JSON only.
api.x.fVersion: Interface version. Present on every successful response.
api.x.fmtP1: Add format=csv to any route and the same rows arrive flattened into columns, with a Content-Disposition filename attached so a browser saves rather than displays them. CSV is a first-class citizen here because it is what people actually load into pandas, R and Excel.
api.x.fmtP2: Paging a CSV. The continuation token cannot live in the body of a CSV, so it lives in the response headers instead: X-Next-Cursor carries the next cursor when one exists, and X-Row-Count carries the number of data rows. You can therefore page a bulk download without parsing a byte of the file. The header value is already URL-encoded — pass it straight back.
api.x.fmtP3: Where CSV and JSON differ. The columns track the JSON fields with two exceptions, both of them omissions: first_seen and last_seen are omitted from the /stations CSV, and upstream_timestamp is omitted from the /latest and raw-measurement CSVs. Everything else is column-for-field identical, pm25_correction_applied_since included: it carries the same date string the JSON does, and an empty cell is simply how CSV spells null — a network we never correct, not a correction date we failed to record.
api.x.fmtP4: One CSV quirk worth knowing. Spreadsheets execute a cell that begins with =, +, - or @, and station names arrive from external feeds, so any such value is prefixed with an apostrophe to render it inert. In practice this affects southern latitudes, which appear as '-8.533623. Strip a leading apostrophe before parsing coordinates numerically.
api.x.heroDeck: Every number on this site comes out of one read-only interface, and that interface is open. Point a browser, a shell, a notebook or a spreadsheet at it and you have the same archive we do — every station, every reading, back to the beginning of the record. This page is the whole manual.
api.x.heroKicker: Public API · Version 1 · No key required
api.x.intDaily: Daily means, with minimum, maximum and sample count where the underlying store holds them. The default, and the right choice for trend work. The date is a WITA calendar day, not a UTC one — see Chapter E.
api.x.intHourly: Hourly means. Native for Nafas and scraped IQAir stations, which publish hourly upstream; bucketed here from the raw snapshots for every other network. Only the bucketed-here case carries the hour's minimum, maximum and sample count — the native ones return null for all three, because upstream gives one number per hour, not a distribution.
api.x.intRaw: Fifteen-minute snapshots exactly as they were fetched, with every companion value the sensor supplied — PM10, PM1, AQI, temperature, humidity, and the upstream timestamp. This is the unaggregated record. Not available for scraped IQAir stations.
api.x.iqsP1: IQAir publishes its city pages hourly, so the stations we scrape from it — every station_id beginning iqs- — have no sub-hourly series to hand you. Asking for interval=raw on one of them returns HTTP 400 with the code no_raw_for_source and the intervals that will work. This is not a gap we can fill by trying harder; the data does not exist at that resolution upstream.
api.x.iqsP2: Everything else about those stations behaves normally, and they carry some of the longest records in the archive — the Umalas station reaches back to November 2024. Use interval=hourly or interval=daily and they behave like any other station.
api.x.licArchive: Published for public-interest research. Free to use, redistribute and build on, with attribution. There is no separate commercial licence to buy and no permission to request — this exists to be used.
api.x.licAttr: Credit both this archive — Bali Air Dispatch, baliair.pages.dev — and the originating network named in each row's source field. The networks did the measuring; we only kept the record.
api.x.licUpstream: Readings originate from independent networks — Nafas, IQAir, PurpleAir, AQICN, OpenAQ, AirGradient, Smart Citizen and Airly — and remain subject to their own terms. This project aggregates and preserves; it does not own the underlying measurements.
api.x.licWarranty: Low-cost sensors are not reference-grade instruments. Values are provided as recorded, without warranty of accuracy or fitness for any purpose. Every response repeats these four statements, so a saved file always carries its own terms.
api.x.metaA: No key · GET only · CORS open
api.x.pCursor: The next_cursor value from the previous response, passed back unmodified. Keyset pagination, so page one thousand costs what page one costs, and rows are never skipped or repeated when new data lands mid-pull.
api.x.pFrom: Start of the window, inclusive. Accepts YYYY-MM-DD, a full ISO-8601 instant, or unix seconds. A bare date is read as UTC midnight.
api.x.pInterval: One of raw, hourly, daily. See Chapter C for what each one actually contains. hourly without a station additionally requires a bounded window — see below.
api.x.pLimit: Rows per page. Anything above the maximum is silently clamped to it; anything unparseable falls back to the default.
api.x.pSource: Return only stations from one network. Matched case-insensitively against the source field — for example nafas, purpleair, iqair, aqicn, openaq, airgradient, smart citizen, airly.
api.x.pSource2: Return only readings from one network, matched case-insensitively against the source field.
api.x.pStation: A station_id taken from /stations. Omit it entirely to pull every station in one paged scan.
api.x.pTo: End of the window, inclusive. Same three formats as from. A bare YYYY-MM-DD is extended to 23:59:59 of that day, so to covers the whole named day at every interval — to=2026-07-30 with interval=raw returns that day's last snapshot, not nothing. The query block echoes the instant actually used.
api.x.quickH: The one line that gets you started
api.x.quickNote: The base URL is https://baliair.pages.dev/api/v1. Requesting it with no path returns a machine-readable index of everything documented on this page — routes, parameters, intervals, caveats and licence — which is the version to trust if this page and the interface ever disagree.
api.x.quickP: Paste this into a terminal. It returns the most recent reading held for every station in the archive.
api.x.r1H: 1 · One station, daily, straight to a CSV file
api.x.r1P: The whole daily record for the Klungkung sensor, saved where a spreadsheet can open it.
api.x.r2H: 2 · Load the daily series into pandas
api.x.r2Note: limit=10000 is the ceiling for a single page. If X-Row-Count comes back equal to your limit there is more behind it — page it with recipe 3. Two things to add before you publish anything off this frame: date here is a WITA calendar day, not a UTC one, and the CSV also carries a samples column worth filtering on — ambient[ambient["samples"] > 1] drops the single-observation daily rows described in Chapter E.
api.x.r2P: Pandas reads the CSV straight off the URL. The one line that normalises suspected_indoor is worth keeping: it makes the filter correct whether pandas parsed the column as a boolean or left it as text.
api.x.r3P: Roughly 140,000 rows, in pages of ten thousand. The cursor arrives in the X-Next-Cursor header already URL-encoded, so it goes straight back into the query string; when the header stops appearing, you are done.
api.x.r4P: Every measurement row carries its own suspected_indoor flag, so most of the time you filter in place. When you need the list itself — to document what you excluded, or to filter a dataset you joined from elsewhere — take it from the catalogue.
api.x.tryFail: The request failed. The interface may be briefly unreachable — try the curl command above.
api.x.tryHint: Same-origin request · nothing leaves this page
appx.x.mApiPointer: The uncorrected figure is published alongside every corrected reading through the public API, so you can verify or reverse this correction on the raw data yourself — the API is documented here.
api.x.corrSinceP: pm25_correction_applied_since is a network policy date, not a claim about any particular row. It says: from this date onward, readings from this station's network are humidity-corrected before publication. It is null for networks we never correct. Rows archived before that date are uncorrected even for a corrected network — the per-row truth is pm25_corrected on a /latest or interval=raw row, which is true exactly when pm25_raw is present.
api.x.staleLabel: "Latest" means latest held, not latest measured
api.x.staleP1: This route returns the newest reading the archive holds for each station. For a sensor that went dark, that reading can be weeks or months old, and it is returned anyway — a station's last known value is legitimately useful. It is simply not current conditions.
api.x.staleP2: age_hours is how old the reading is, in hours, at the moment the response was generated. stale is true when that exceeds 24 hours. A real row from this route, captured while writing this page:
api.x.staleP3: That is a fifty-nine-day-old figure of 168 µg/m³. Average it into an island-wide "right now" number and you have published a fiction. Filter on stale, or set your own threshold from age_hours, before you treat any of these rows as live.
api.x.ep4note3: Bulk raw is the one asymmetry. interval=raw reads the sub-hourly snapshot store, which is the only place sub-hourly data exists. Scraped IQAir stations therefore never appear in a raw pull — they have no raw series at any level, named or not.
api.x.windowP: interval=hourly without a station has to aggregate before it can page, so limit bounds the response but not the work. That combination therefore requires both from and to, spanning at most 31 days. Omit either and you get window_required; exceed the span and you get window_too_large. Both are HTTP 400. Name a single station and neither limit applies; raw and daily bulk scans are unbounded.
api.x.hdrP: Four headers carry information the body does not. Note that only X-Next-Cursor and X-Row-Count are listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, so those two are the ones browser JavaScript can actually read cross-origin; X-Cache is visible to curl and to servers, not to fetch().
api.x.hX1: On a CSV /measurements response, the continuation token — the CSV equivalent of next_cursor. Absent when there is no further page. Already URL-encoded; pass it straight back. Not set on JSON responses, which carry next_cursor in the body instead.
api.x.hX2: On a CSV /measurements response, the number of data rows written, so you can detect a full page without parsing the file.
api.x.hX3: HIT when the response came out of the edge cache rather than the database. The request that actually ran the query carries no X-Cache header at all, so treat "absent" as the miss case.
api.x.hX4: On CSV responses only: attachment with a generated filename, so a browser saves the file rather than rendering it.
api.x.errWindowRequired: interval=hourly was requested without a station and without both from and to. Bound the window to at most 31 days, or name one station.
api.x.errWindowTooLarge: interval=hourly without a station, over a window longer than 31 days. Split the pull into 31-day requests, or name one station.
api.x.cP3: Which basis the dates are on. Every /measurements response also carries date_basis, which is "WITA (UTC+8) calendar day" when the rows are daily and "UTC instant" when they are hourly or raw. It is there so a script never has to infer the boundary from the interval it asked for.
api.x.fDateBasis: Which calendar the row keys are on: "WITA (UTC+8) calendar day" for interval=daily, "UTC instant" for hourly and raw. /measurements only.
api.x.fMessage: A human sentence explaining the failure. Present only on errors. Show it; branch on error.
api.x.fCorrectionSince: The date from which this station's network has its PM2.5 humidity-corrected before publication, or null for a network we never correct. A statement about network policy, not about any individual row: readings archived before this date are uncorrected even here. For per-row truth use pm25_corrected on a /latest or interval=raw row.
api.x.fSourceRow: The network the reading originated from. Carried on every /latest row and every /measurements row at every interval, so attribution never needs a join back to /stations. This is the name to credit.
api.x.fAgeHours: How old the reading was, in hours to one decimal, at the moment the response was generated. /latest only.
api.x.fStale: true when age_hours exceeds 24, and also when the station has no usable timestamp at all. /latest only. Read it before treating a row as current conditions.
api.x.fSourceRow2: The network the bucket's readings came from. Carried on every aggregate row; this is the name to credit.
api.x.caveat2Label: 2 · /latest is the newest reading held, not the newest reading taken
api.x.caveat2P1: There is no freshness filter on /latest. Every station the archive holds a usable value for gets a row, including sensors that stopped reporting months ago, and their last known value is returned as-is. Read literally as "conditions now", that route will hand you readings that are weeks old alongside readings that are minutes old, in the same array, indistinguishable by value.
api.x.caveat2P2: Which is why every row carries age_hours and stale. stale is true past 24 hours; a large minority of the stations in a typical response are over it, and the oldest run to well past a thousand hours. Filter on stale, or set your own threshold from age_hours, before you average anything from this route. For a defensible current-conditions figure, prefer a bounded /measurements window over /latest altogether.
api.x.caveat3Label: 3 · A daily row can be one reading wearing a mean's clothes
api.x.caveat3P1: samples is how many observations went into an aggregate. On older backfilled daily rows it is frequently 1 — and a large share of the daily series is in that state. Where the row was backfilled from a single snapshot, the minimum, the maximum and the mean are then all the same number:
api.x.caveat3P2: That is not a daily average of Bali's air; it is one instant, presented in the shape of a daily average. Where the row was backfilled from an upstream daily summary instead, samples is still 1 while the min and max do differ — the count means one record ingested, not one sensor reading. Either way, check samples before you plot a daily series, and where precision matters prefer interval=raw or interval=hourly, which are computed from the snapshots themselves. A null is a different case again: that store holds no count, so you cannot tell how thin the row is.
api.x.caveat6: Gaps are real. A sensor that went silent has no rows for that period — not a repeated last value, not a zero, not an interpolation. If your chart has a hole in it, that hole is the truth: nobody was measuring. This matters for Bali specifically, because several of the longest-running stations in the record went dark and stayed dark. Do not fill forward without saying so, and never treat a missing row as a clean-air row.
api.x.caveat7: These are not reference instruments. Low-cost sensors drift, disagree with each other, and are affected by humidity and by their own siting. Values are published as recorded, without warranty of accuracy or fitness for any purpose. They are good enough to establish patterns, trends and magnitudes, and they are what exists — Bali has almost no regulatory monitoring. Treat them as evidence of what the air is doing, not as calibrated measurement, and say so in whatever you publish.
home.x.legReports: Dashed circle = area with community burning reports, sized by count, fading over 30 days
home.x.locateUnsupported: Location is unavailable in this browser

Locations are published at village (desa) level by the source project, deliberately, so no report points at a specific property. These are citizen observations, not sensor readings, and play no part in any air-quality statistic on this site.
